newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac to step in as French poll race tightens.
newsitem.headline: Chirac to step in as French poll race tightens.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac was poised on Tuesday to step into France's election battle, drawing warnings from leftist opponents that this would be another risky gamble after his decision to call a snap poll.

As surveys showed the left snapping at the heels of the ruling centre-right and more than one third of voters still undecided ahead of the May 25/June 1 election, Chirac's office might announce details of his intervention.
While fellow conservatives urged Chirac to enter the fray to tip the balance, former interior minister Charles Pasqua, a rightist dissident, advised him against getting too involved in the campaign.
Political sources said the 64-year-old president might write an opinion article for various provincial newspapers on Wednesday, the second anniversary of his own election.
But his political opponents said such a move by Chirac would jeopardise the remainder of his seven-year term should the left win the election.
"The more he gets involved in the campaign, the more he risks reducing his authority," said leftist Jean-Pierre Chevenement, a former defence minister.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, seen in one opinion poll as currently the best campaigner, said he could not see "what he could tell us that could weigh in the election."
Far-rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen said Chirac had turned the election into a plebiscite and would have to resign if his supporters lost.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe, campaigning in eastern France, appealed to the undecided, urging them to return the centre-right with a strong majority in order to reinforce Chirac's authority and France's weight in Europe.

The latest opinion polls showed the two sides neck-and-neck. A BVA survey gave the conservatives 40 percent of voting intentions, half a point ahead of the combined left, while a Louis Harris poll saw them level on 38 percent.

Juppe accused the Socialists of making unrealistic spending proposals and told voters to remember that they were routed in the last parliamentary election four years ago "quite simply because they had failed."

Jospin accused the conservatives of borrowing from the Socialist platform and, acknowledging past Socialist failures, he urged voters to punish the conservatives as they had punished the left in 1993.
"If (voters) use the same criteria to pass judgment on the ruling coalition, its achievements and behaviour, the outcome should not be in doubt," he said.
Plans for a European single currency remained high among campaign issues highlighted by politicians, although a Sofres opinion poll suggested this was way down in the list of voters' concerns.

The survey said unemployment topped the list, followed by social inequalities. The status of immigrants, one of the main campaign issues for Le Pen's National Front, was eighth on the list with the single currency on ninth.
